questions.stem: Which antibiotic binds the same ribosomal subunit as tetracycline?
questions.explanation: Tetracyclines and aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) bind the 30S subunit. A: Macrolides act on 50S. B: Clindamycin acts on 50S. C: Linezolid acts on 50S. D: Chloramphenicol acts on 50S.

questions.stem: Co-trimoxazole combines a sulfonamide with trimethoprim. Which enzyme does the trimethoprim component inhibit?
questions.explanation: Trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase (dihydrofolic → tetrahydrofolic acid); with sulfonamides it blocks two sequential folate steps. A: Sulfonamides (PABA analogs) inhibit this earlier step (slide name; standard name dihydropteroate synthase). C: Quinolones inhibit DNA gyrase. D: Rifampicin inhibits RNA polymerase. E: β-lactams inhibit transpeptidase.

questions.stem: Why is nafcillin effective against penicillinase-producing S. aureus while penicillin G is not?

options.A: It binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini instead of PBPs
options.C: Its bulky R side chain blocks β-lactamase access to the β-lactam ring
options.D: It is always given with clavulanic acid
options.E: It binds the altered PBP encoded by mecA

questions.explanation: Steric hindrance from the bulky R group protects the β-lactam ring, so nafcillin is used for S. aureus (except MRSA). A: That is vancomycin. B: That ring is the cephalosporin structure. D: Clavulanate is paired with amoxicillin (Augmentin), not needed for nafcillin. E: mecA-altered PBP is exactly why MRSA resists nafcillin.
Ceftaroline (5th generation) covers MRSA but not Pseudomonas. A: Cefazolin is 1st generation. C: Cefaclor is 2nd. D: Ceftriaxone is 3rd. E: Cefepime is 4th; it doesn't cover MRSA.

questions.stem: During an epidemic of cerebrospinal meningitis, healthy close contacts are given oral rifampicin. This use is best described as:
questions.explanation: Chemoprophylaxis = antimicrobials to prevent infection in people not yet infected (also: amoxicillin before dental extraction in heart disease, preoperative use). B: Combinations to prevent resistance are used in TB. C: Superinfection is overgrowth of resistant flora (oral Candida, C. difficile). D: Synergy means two drugs together (e.g. penicillin + aminoglycoside). E: The contacts are not ill.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with atypical pneumonia fails amoxicillin. Cold agglutinins are positive. Why did amoxicillin fail?

options.A: The organism lacks a cell wall
options.B: The organism carries a β-lactamase R plasmid
options.E: The organism has an mecA-altered PBP

questions.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae naturally lacks a cell wall, so β-lactams have no target (non-genetic resistance by loss of target structure). B: β-lactamase is genetic resistance in wall-bearing bacteria. C: 30S changes affect aminoglycosides/tetracyclines. D: Dormancy is the M. tuberculosis example of non-genetic resistance. E: mecA is the MRSA mechanism.

questions.stem: In an E-test (epsilometer) on an inoculated agar plate, how is the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) read?

options.A: The diameter of the inhibition zone around a disc, in mm
options.B: Comparison of zone size with CLSI tables as S/I/R
options.C: The highest concentration printed on the strip
options.D: The point where the elliptical inhibition zone meets the strip
options.E: The concentration at the tip of the strip after 24 h

questions.explanation: The strip carries an antibiotic gradient; after 24 h at 37 °C a tear-drop zone forms and the zone edge's intersection with the strip is the MIC. A: That is Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion. B: That is how disc diffusion is interpreted. C: The highest concentration is not the MIC. E: The tip has no special meaning; the intersection point does.

questions.stem: Ciprofloxacin kills bacteria by inhibiting which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Quinolones (nalidixic acid, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) inhibit DNA gyrase and block DNA synthesis. A: Rifampicin inhibits RNA polymerase. B: Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. D: β-lactams inhibit transpeptidase. E: Vancomycin physically obstructs glycosyltransferase.

questions.stem: A Staphylococcus aureus isolate is resistant to methicillin and all other β-lactams, though β-lactamase inhibitors do not restore activity. What is the resistance mechanism?

options.C: Loss of the cell wall target
options.D: Decreased permeability of the outer membrane
options.E: Altered penicillin-binding protein from a mecA mutation

questions.explanation: MRSA resists by modifying the target: mecA alters the PBP so β-lactams no longer bind (vancomycin or ceftaroline are used). A: A β-lactamase inhibitor would restore activity. B: Efflux pumps are the quinolone example. C: Loss of target is Mycoplasma. D: S. aureus is Gram-positive and has no outer membrane.
